title: AI’s recursive self-improvement might not come so quickly after all
gist: A Princeton-led study using a new 'shadow evaluation' method found that AI agents can do the engineering of AI research but lack the creativity and judgment to produce publishable original work—both agent-written papers were rejected by their original human authors—suggesting hyped recursive-self-improvement timelines are running ahead of the evidence.

insights.claim: The AI industry's boldest current promise is that AI will soon improve itself with almost no human oversight, with forecasts predicting recursive self-improvement is on the horizon.
insights.speaker: Michelle Kim
insights.so_what: Recursive self-improvement is the assumption underpinning the most explosive AI-progress forecasts and valuations, so evidence against it is materially bearish.
insights.quote: The AI industry’s boldest promise right now is that AI will soon improve itself, with almost no need for human oversight.

insights.claim: AI companies have every incentive to build self-accelerating AI, with OpenAI making an automated AI researcher an explicit goal and Anthropic identifying self-improving AI as the industry's next milestone.
insights.speaker: Michelle Kim
insights.so_what: The strategic priority both labs place on self-improvement means near-term progress claims will keep coming regardless of current gaps.
insights.locator: AI companies do have every incentive

insights.claim: A Princeton-led team led by Peter Kirgis and Sayash Kapoor found AI agents could solve the engineering problems of AI research but lacked the judgment and creativity to produce original research at the caliber of top machine-learning conference papers.
insights.speaker: Michelle Kim
insights.so_what: Separates automatable engineering from non-automatable research judgment, the key bottleneck for self-improvement timelines.

insights.claim: The researchers introduced 'shadow evaluation,' requiring an AI to answer a research question from a high-quality unpublished paper so the agent cannot memorize answers from training data or find them online.
insights.speaker: Michelle Kim
insights.so_what: A novel evaluation design that tests open-ended research ability more richly than checkable-answer benchmarks.
insights.locator: To test agents on those kinds of skills

insights.claim: Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.8 on OpenClaw was given six days, $3,000 in API credits, a GPU budget, virtual computers, and web access to produce publishable papers on two unpublished NeurIPS 2026 submissions, and the original authors rejected both.
insights.speaker: Michelle Kim
insights.so_what: A concrete, well-resourced test where a frontier model failed the research-quality bar, grounding the skeptical thesis.
insights.locator: The agents were given six days

insights.claim: The agents were unambiguously bad at the research itself—running bizarre experiments on tiny synthetic datasets, struggling to write intelligibly, and making no novel contribution—despite handling all the required engineering.
insights.speaker: Michelle Kim
insights.so_what: The failure mode is judgment and creativity, not compute or engineering, which is far harder to fix with scale.
insights.quote: On the other hand, the agents were unambiguously bad at carrying out the research itself.
insights.locator: The agents were capable of all the engineering

insights.claim: The agents committed to unpromising approaches too quickly, rejected ambitious hypotheses on very limited data, and could make small pivots but could not fundamentally rethink or restart their approach.
insights.speaker: Michelle Kim
insights.so_what: Inability to backtrack and explore is a core research skill gap that narrow-task scaling may not address.

insights.claim: The agents failed to incorporate feedback from subagents or external reviewing tools, instead narrowing claims and adding caveats rather than revising methodology, and couldn't manage tokens, compute, time, or instructions.
insights.speaker: Michelle Kim
insights.so_what: Poor resource and feedback handling limits agents' autonomy in exactly the open-ended settings self-improvement requires.
insights.locator: The agents also failed to incorporate feedback

insights.claim: Despite their failures, the agents did not engage in reward hacking, and when subagents occasionally hallucinated or misrepresented results, the orchestrator agent caught them.
insights.speaker: Michelle Kim
insights.so_what: A rare positive safety signal: the failure was competence, not deception, easing one class of misbehavior concern.

insights.claim: Kapoor argues models excel at research engineering but not open-ended research because reinforcement learning drills them on tasks whose success can be checked automatically, and it is harder to build training environments for open-ended tasks.
insights.speaker: Michelle Kim
insights.so_what: Roots the capability gap in the training paradigm itself, implying it won't close automatically with more of the same.
insights.quote: But it’s harder to create environments to train these models when the task itself is open-ended.
insights.locator: The reason AI models are good at research engineering

insights.claim: AI progress may bifurcate, with systems racing ahead on narrow scorable tasks while advancing slowly on open-ended research.
insights.speaker: Michelle Kim
insights.so_what: A bifurcated trajectory would mean benchmark gains overstate real progress toward autonomous research.
insights.locator: On the other hand, it’s possible that AI progress

themes.theme: Industry corroboration and the open question

insights.claim: Anthropic cofounder Jack Clark wrote that AI systems' 'certain absence of valuable, intuitive creativity' and 'rote, formulaic thinking' is a bearish signal on short recursive-self-improvement timelines, echoing what the company found automating AI safety research.
insights.speaker: Michelle Kim
insights.so_what: An insider from a leading lab publicly tempering timelines lends the skeptical finding unusual credibility.
insights.quote: There’s a certain absence of valuable, intuitive creativity in today’s AI systems

insights.claim: In June Anthropic published a blog post titled 'When AI Builds Itself' and in July OpenAI advertised that GPT-5.6 Sol helped post-train a smaller model, saving researchers weeks—optimistic public statements the new finding may quietly contradict.
insights.speaker: Michelle Kim
insights.so_what: Highlights a gap between labs' promotional claims and internal reality that investors should weigh.
insights.locator: In June, Anthropic published a blog post

insights.claim: The trillion-dollar open question is how crucial open-ended research is to recursive self-improvement, since Kapoor notes the field's biggest advances like transformers required creative leaps, while others hypothesize everything needed is already there.
insights.speaker: Michelle Kim
insights.so_what: Whether creative leaps are required determines if narrow-task scaling alone can reach transformative AI—the central investment debate.
insights.quote: That’s frankly the trillion-dollar question right now.
